subjects.displayTitle: Addressing Christians: the challenge of recognition
subjects.introduction: Which is the better temple, Bahá’u’lláh asks the concourse of the Son, the one built of clay or the one built by the hands of the Lord’s power, the living human being? With that question he addresses Christians in their own language: the gate of reunion opened, John sent once more to cry in the wilderness, the Father come, bells pealing out his remembrance, Bethlehem itself answering the call. The claim is unmistakably Bahá’í, that fidelity to Christ asks for the recognition of a further revelation, and it is pressed with urgency upon the Pope, upon monks and upon all who read the Gospel. One thread deserves particular attention: Jesus’ saying that he had many things to tell his disciples which they could not yet bear, and his promise of the Spirit of truth, which Bahá’u’lláh reads as fulfilled in his own Word [1]. The convictions of those addressed deserve to be taken as seriously as the proclamation itself. From here the journey leads to Christ and Christianity, to the story of Christian rejection of Bahá’u’lláh, and to the proclamations addressed to Jews, Muslims, kings and the peoples of the world.
subjects.arc: Open with the living human temple, develop the summons to recognition, and bring scriptural promises into conversation with response, suffering, and service.

order.why: Introduce the address to the Pope through the figures of John and the returning Lord.
shortened: O Pope!  Rend the veils asunder.  He Who is the Lord of Lords is come overshadowed with clouds, and the decree hath been fulfilled by God, the Almighty, the Unrestrained.

O followers of the Son!  We have once again sent John unto you, and He, verily, hath cried out in the wilderness of the Bayan:  O peoples of the world!  Cleanse your eyes!  The Day whereon ye can behold the Promised One and attain unto Him hath drawn nigh!

order.why: Begin with the contrast between a living temple and a building.
Let the opened gate turn that image into an invitation.
Hear the summons to monks within their familiar language of worship.
Turn explicitly to the reading of the Gospel.
Examine the relationship asserted between Christ and the Father.
Pause over the question addressed to those who doubt.
Read the claim of fulfillment through the language of descent from heaven.
shortened: The Gospel exclaims: "He has come from heaven, He through Whose mention God, the Lord of the seen and unseen, adorned His Book."

order.why: Consider the description of heaven as a realm of proof.
Hear the Spirit announce the promised revelation.
shortened: And the Spirit calls out: "O people of the Gospel! By God, the Promised One has come from the heaven of proof with His most great glory. Fear God and deny not Him Who was promised you in the Psalms and Tablets."

order.why: Directly addresses the people of the Gospel with the announcement that the promised return has come.
Allow the personified Gospel to voice the claim.
Explore the further personification of Bethlehem.
shortened: Then the Call was raised from Bethlehem saying: "At Thy service, O Thou through Whom the ocean of knowledge surged before the faces of all religions!

order.why: Connect the Kingdom with the imagery of Moses’ tabernacle.
Reflect on the distance between an offered gift and its reception.
Bring suffering into the account of proclamation.
shortened: O people of the Son! The Kingdom hath been adorned with My Name, and the Dominion with My sovereignty, and the Spirit lamenteth by reason of that which hath befallen Me at the hands of the oppressors.

order.why: Consider the purpose of renewed sacrifice in the uniting of peoples.
Read the reported appeal to the friends of Christ.
shortened: O friends of Jesus Christ!  know that the promises of nineteen hundred years ago are today fulfilled, and that the Son of Man is here in "the Kingdom of His Father," holding out His loving arms toward the North, South, East and West, while His Voice is calling, ever calling:

"O people!  The Doors of the Kingdom are opened; the Sun of Truth is shining upon the world; the Fountains of Life are flowing; the Daysprings of Mercy have appeared; the Greatest and Most Glorious Light is now manifest to illuminate the hearts of men.

order.why: End the linked texts with an account of speaking in churches.
shortened: Yesterday I spoke at length in two great churches before thousands of people. The Blessed Cause and the prophethood of Muhammad, peace be upon Him, were proven with utmost clarity. Glory be to God! Through the assistance and favor of the Blessed Beauty, not a single person raised any objection. Rather, all listened in complete silence and stillness.

order.why: Revisit the promise of further teaching through the address to followers of the Son.
shortened: The Father is come, and that which ye were promised in the Kingdom is fulfilled! This is the Word which the Son concealed, when to those around Him He said: "Ye cannot bear it now." And when the appointed time was fulfilled and the Hour had struck, the Word shone forth above the horizon of the Will of God. Beware, O followers of the Son, that ye cast it not behind your backs.

order.why: Close with the relationship between worship, human life, and responding to the present day.

questions: How does the image of the human temple change the meaning of responding to a religious summons?
What kinds of continuity with Christ do these selections claim, and what would a reader need to investigate to assess those claims?
How does reading John 16 in its own setting enrich or complicate the interpretation offered here?
What habits could make a conversation about fulfillment both candid about disagreement and receptive to another person’s understanding?

neighbors.invitation: Follow the example of Elijah and John the Baptist into the question of return.
Consider how to pursue differences of interpretation without quarrelling.
Connect recognition with putting Christ’s teachings into action.

references.label: 1 · John 16:12–15 (King James Version)
references.note: Jesus speaks of teaching his disciples cannot yet bear, of guidance through the Spirit of truth, and of the relationship of that guidance to himself and the Father. Compare this passage with the compilation’s appeals to further revelation. The comparison identifies a shared text and a question of interpretation; it does not assume that Christian and Bahá’í readers agree on the fulfillment of the promise.

subjects.displayTitle: Addressing Jews: covenant, promise, and recognition
subjects.introduction: Carmel is told to call out to Zion with joyful tidings: the One hidden from mortal eyes has come. Addressing the people of the Torah, Bahá’u’lláh speaks entirely in their inherited language. He announces the promise made to the House of David, declares that the Ten Words have been revealed in a single Word, names Abraham the Friend and Moses the Interlocutor, and lets the Mount and the burning Tree themselves cry out that the Lord is here. The tone moves between an invitation to rejoice and the challenge of how long a people can sleep. Isaiah’s vision of a shoot from Jesse bringing righteous judgment for the poor, peace among the creatures and knowledge of God filling the earth gives the hope its first scriptural setting [1]. This is a Bahá’í understanding of fulfilment, best weighed beside Jewish interpretations of the same scriptures heard on their own terms. From here one may turn to the Torah and the Jewish people themselves, and to the parallel calls addressed to Christians and to Muslims.
subjects.arc: Begin with the call from Carmel to Zion, follow covenantal and prophetic images, and move from joyful announcement to the work of recognition.

order.why: Hear the mount and tree personify recognition.
Open with the vivid call from Carmel to Zion.
shortened: Call out to Zion, O Carmel, and announce the joyful tidings: He that was hidden from mortal eyes is come! His all-conquering sovereignty is manifest; His all-encompassing splendor is revealed.

order.why: Connect the announcement with the promise to the House of David.
shortened: Then turn thy gaze unto the concourse of the Torah and say: He hath come unto you - the Sovereign of Names and Attributes, within Whose grasp lieth the kingdom of verses, and there hath appeared at His right hand that which was promised unto you of the House of David. Indeed, He is the Promised One in your midst, and now He calleth unto you from the right of the throne of your Lord, the Loving.

order.why: Turn to Moses, the commandments, and the places of remembrance.
Bring the appeal to Ezekiel and Sinai into the sequence.
Return to David’s throne as an image of revelation.
Pause over the direct invitation to rejoice.
Read the encouragement addressed to those who have responded.
shortened: Praise be to God that in this Most Great Cycle the glance of grace encompasses Israel so that all the promises of the Prophets regarding them may be fulfilled in the world of existence and witness. O friends of Israel! His Holiness Moses offers praise in the Kingdom of sanctification for your enkindlement and attraction, and the denizens of the realm of might offer commendation, and the divines offer description, and the Concourse on High cry out at every moment "Blessed are ye! Blessed are ye!"

order.why: Follow the good tidings associated with Abraham and Moses.
shortened: Say: O concourse of the Torah! The Friend hath appeared and the Interlocutor hath come, both giving glad tidings of that which hath appeared and shone forth from the horizon of God's Will, the All-Knowing, the All-Informed.

order.why: Consider what it means to remember an inherited covenant.
Examine the call to detachment addressed to the heirs of that inheritance.
Read the summons to the people of Moses.
Consider the question of recognizing the appointed time.
shortened: O servant! Say to the concourse of the Jews: Your appointed time hath been fulfilled - where then is the Promised One? Bring Him forth if ye be of the learned!

order.why: Face the intimate contrast between belonging and failing to recognize.
Directly addresses the Jews and identifies the present Manifestation with the return of Jesus.
Ask how signs become grounds for recognition or doubt.
shortened: O people of the Torah, the signs of God have filled the horizons while you remain in doubt and discord. How long will you play with your vain imaginings?

order.why: Complete the linked readings with the promise of renewing breezes.
Revisit covenant through the explicitly named patriarchs and Jerusalem.
Hear the call issued from the prison of ‘Akká.
shortened: O heir of Moses! Hear the call of the Lord of Hosts which hath been raised in the world of creation from the prison of Akka, summoning you to His most glorious horizon.

order.why: Close with the claim of renewed recognition of the beauty associated with Moses.
shortened: Fear God and deny not Him Who was promised you in the Psalms and Tablets." And Moses calls out: "He Whose beauty I was prevented from beholding has appeared. Hasten, O people of the Torah, unto the good-pleasure of God, the Almighty, the Unconstrained." And the Point of the Bayan laments and says: "O My servants! We counseled you in all Our Books, nay in every leaf, to believe in Him and His verses, yet you committed that which caused all things to lament."

order.why: Examine the Torah and throne imagery used to declare fulfillment.

questions: What different dimensions of hope are carried by the covenant, throne, mountain, and tree in these passages?
How does Isaiah’s attention to judgment, peace, and knowledge help distinguish the content of a promise from the question of who fulfills it?
What could faithful remembrance contribute to openness, and when might a settled expectation make recognition difficult?
How might Jewish and Bahá’í readers explore these claims together while giving each tradition’s interpretation a fair hearing?

neighbors.invitation: Compare the use of a living temple with these covenantal images.
Explore how another address connects scriptural inheritance with a present response.
Reflect on preserving fellowship while interpretations differ.

references.label: 1 · Isaiah 11:1–9 (JPS 1917 translation, Mechon Mamre)
references.note: The chapter joins the image of a shoot from Jesse with righteous judgment for the poor, faithfulness, peaceful animal life, and knowledge of God. Read these verses first within their Jewish scriptural setting, then compare the compilation’s images of Davidic promise and divine recognition. The ethical substance of hope provides a fruitful point of inquiry without presuming agreement about a later claimant.

subjects.displayTitle: Addressing Muslims: scripture, fairness, and response
subjects.introduction: Do you read the Qur’án and yet object to its Revealer? Bahá’u’lláh puts the question to the people of the Furqán with a directness that assumes they love the Book. His appeal is to the fairness such love ought to produce: ponder a single verse honestly, and the straight path will open; judge with equity rather than from inherited expectation or self-interest. The Báb, before Him, had called the people of Mecca to recognise a proof descended in tablets from a preserved Book, and had warned against a faith built on conjecture. Behind the urgency stands the day when all shall stand before the Lord of the worlds. The Qur’án itself asks that disagreement with the People of the Book be conducted in the best manner, with the one God acknowledged on both sides, a discipline worth carrying into any such encounter [1]. Reading these addresses honestly means weighing the evidence offered and the fairness of one’s own response, and then turning to Muhammad, the Seal of the Prophets, to the Faith of Islam itself, and to the parallel calls addressed to Christians and to Jews.
subjects.arc: Begin with the responsibility of fair judgment, examine the appeal to scripture, and then hear the proclamations and warnings that make response urgent.

order.why: Connect the language of remembrance with responsibility in judgment.
shortened: Say: O people of the Qur'an, know ye your station! Ye made mention of Me throughout ages and centuries, yet when the fingers of might rent asunder the veils and shrouds, ye pronounced judgment against Me with such tyranny as caused the pillars to tremble.

order.why: Open with the explicit appeal to judge fairly.
Examine the tension between reading scripture and opposing its claimed fulfillment.
Focus the inquiry on pondering a verse of the Qur’án.
shortened: If the followers of the Qur'an would but ponder a single verse, they would find their way to the Straight Path and the Most Great Announcement.

order.why: Read the Báb’s proclamation and appeal to revealed writings as proof.
Consider the warning against building a response upon conjecture. Close with the Báb’s account of the relationship between the Imams, the Prophet, and the Qur’án.
shortened: O people of Islam! After one thousand two hundred and seventy years have passed, when one of our followers, whose name is mentioned by our name in your religion and within the bounds of your faith, pronounces judgment concerning your departure from your religion - because you follow conjecture rather than truth while supposing you do well - if this be your station before one of our followers, how must it be before Us or before God, your Lord and our Lord?

order.why: Explore the claim that religious ordinances culminate in a divine purpose.
Bring the day of standing before God into view.
Consider the mount of knowledge and the straight path.
Hear the announcement that the hidden has become manifest.
Read the personified Qur’án as a witness within the proclamation.
shortened: And the Qur'an calls humanity unto the Truth Who was promised by the Most Exalted Pen in a preserved tablet.

order.why: Examine the assertion that scriptural promises have been fulfilled.
shortened: O people of the Furqan! By God, that which ye were promised in the Book hath appeared. Fear ye God and deny not the Cause of God when it hath appeared with the truth, and dispute not the signs of God when they have been sent down from this heaven. Turn ye unto God, your Ancient Lord.

order.why: An extended direct address to the people of the Quran urging recognition, unity and striving with wisdom.
Pause over the announcement of the All-Merciful.
Hear that announcement from the setting of imprisonment.
shortened: Say: O people of the Furqan! Hearken unto the call of your Lord, the All-Merciful. Verily it hath been raised in the prison before the faces of all religions. Follow not your selfish desires, but follow Him Who calleth you unto God, the One, the All-Informed.

order.why: Consider how desire can obstruct the reception of a gift.
shortened: O people of the Furqan (Qur'an), fear God and follow not your vain desires. He guides you to the Dawning-Place of lights. Cast aside what you possess and take what is with God, the Lord of all men.

order.why: Examine the image of setting the Book aside.
Turn from private refusal to the responsibility of barring others.
Complete the linked readings with the lament over denial.

questions: What does fair judgment require when a claim challenges a reader’s understanding of their own scripture?
How do the selections distinguish evidence, inherited expectation, and self-interest in forming a response?
What does Qur’án 29:46 contribute to the manner of a difficult interreligious conversation, and how should its qualification concerning injustice be considered?
How might the neighboring study of prophetic finality help make the disagreement more specific and the inquiry more productive?

neighbors.invitation: Examine an explicit affirmation of Muhammad’s station alongside the language of fulfillment.
Compare another address that calls religious leaders to examine a claim.
Consider the place of remembered inheritance in recognition.

references.label: 1 · Qur’án 29:46 (parallel translations, Quranic Arabic Corpus)
references.note: This verse counsels engagement with the People of the Book in the best manner, with an exception concerning those who act unjustly, and affirms belief in revelation and the one God. It supplies an Islamic scriptural resource for thinking about how religious disagreement is conducted. Its original addressees and direction of address differ from this compilation’s proclamation to Muslims; the comparison concerns the discipline of conversation.

subjects.displayTitle: The return of Christ: expectation and recognition
subjects.introduction: When shall these things be, the disciples asked, and the answer they were given has been argued over ever since: the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with power, after sun and moon are darkened. Bahá’u’lláh and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá read those signs as spiritual, not astronomical. Christ came from heaven the first time, yet He was born of Mary; heaven is the world of divinity, not a region above the sky, and the Christ who returns is the same divine reality rising and setting in each cycle, as Elijah returned in John the Baptist without John being Elijah in person. Acts preserves the promise, given as a cloud hides Jesus from sight, that He will come in like manner [1], and Matthew records the disciples grasping that Elijah had already come unnoticed [2]; both keep the interpretive question honest. The Bahá’í claim is explicit, that the promise was fulfilled in the Báb and Bahá’u’lláh, and it asks what recognition would demand of conduct as well as belief. The road leads on to the resurrection of Christ, to Christian doctrine and practice, and to the return of the Manifestations of God.
subjects.arc: Begin with the disciples’ question, explore the language of heaven and return, and move toward the explicit Bahá’í interpretation and the demands of recognition.

order.why: Examine the dramatic signs in the Gospel account.
shortened: It is recorded in the Sacred Scriptures that Christ will return and that His return is conditioned upon the fulfilment of certain signs: When He returns, He will be attended by those signs. Among them: "The sun shall be darkened, and the moon shall not give her light, and the stars shall fall from heaven." At that time "all the tribes of the earth" shall "mourn" and lament, and "the sign of the Son of man" shall appear "in heaven", "and they shall see the Son of man coming in the clouds of heaven with power and great glory".

order.why: Consider return as renewed spiritual illumination.
Start with the question the disciples themselves ask. Return to the supplied Gospel imagery in its preserved excerpt.
shortened: Afterwards, the companions and disciples of Jesus asked Him concerning those signs that must needs signalize the return of His manifestation. When, they asked, shall these things be? Several times they questioned that peerless Beauty, and, every time He made reply, He set forth a special sign that should herald the advent of the promised Dispensation.

And He saith: at that time, all the peoples and kindreds that dwell on earth shall bewail and lament, and they shall see that divine Beauty coming from heaven, riding upon the clouds with power, grandeur, and magnificence, sending His angels with a great sound of a trumpet.

order.why: Continue with the imagery of darkened lights and clouds.
shortened: Verily the Suns are eclipsed, the luminaries are darkened, the stars are scattered and the Son of Man hath come upon the clouds of Heaven with power and great glory, sending His messengers and hosts with the sounds of the Wonderful Trumpet.

order.why: Set visible expectations beside the image of an unexpected arrival.
shortened: As He saith in the Gospel, My coming is even as when the thief is in the house, and the goodman of the house watcheth not.

order.why: Read the discussion of waiting for a descent from the spatial sky.
shortened: Christ says--"I will come from heaven"--but which heaven is not appointed. Just as He formerly came from heaven, and yet He was born, the second coming will be likewise. But these (people) are expecting Him to come just as a thunder bolt from heaven, and when they did not find this (to be so) and found He was born, it was a veil to them. This time also He has come from heaven, but through the womb.
By heaven is meant the World of Divinity. The meaning is this; that He has the physical body, but His reality is from the Divine Realm. He is not of the contingent world, but of that of Divinity.

order.why: Ask what descent from heaven means in relation to birth from Mary.
Revisit that question in a reported conversation.
shortened: One of the great signs is "I will descend from heaven," and at the present time the Christians are awaiting the same. Jesus Christ, in His first appearance, came from Heaven, although He really came from the womb of Mary.  He said no one can ascend to Heaven except He is come from heaven. He came from the womb of Mary, although in reality He descended from Heaven.

order.why: Introduce Elijah and John as an interpretive example.
Explains return through the example of John and Elijah as spiritual continuity rather than the same soul and body.
Develop the distinction between divine reality and material appearance.
shortened: He shall come with the Kingdom of God and His power which hath surrounded the world. This power (or reign) is in the world of hearts and spirits and not in that of matter (or bodies).

Verily Christ came with His Kingdom from the beginning which hath no beginning and will come with His Kingdom to the eternity of eternities, inasmuch as in this sense Christ is an expression of the divine reality, the simple essence and heavenly entity which hath no beginning or ending. It hath appearance, arising and manifestation and setting in each of the cycles.

order.why: Read a further account of continuity across cycles.
shortened: "Is this what is meant by the Second Coming of Christ?" "Christ is an Expression of the Divine Reality, the Single Essence and Heavenly Entity, which hath no beginning or ending. It has appearance, arising, and manifestation and setting in each one of the Cycles."

order.why: Relate spiritual continuity to appearance in a human body.
shortened: They now believe that Christ will come from heaven in a cloud. Christ has come from heaven, but in a body just as Jesus did.

order.why: Explore the clouds of the heart and the conditions of recognition.
Pause over the image of the descending New Jerusalem.
shortened: The New Jerusalem has descended from heaven!

order.why: Hear the direct declaration of return.
shortened: Verily, He Who was raised to heaven hath come with the truth and giveth glad tidings unto the people of this Revelation whereby the eyes of the Concourse on High and those who circle round the Throne have been solaced through this Most Great Name.

order.why: Read the accompanying image of clouds and heavenly hosts.
Consider the challenge of denial despite a claimed return.
shortened: O son of man! The Pen of the All-Merciful maketh mention of thee in the Most Great Prison and saith: We gave the glad-tidings of the coming of the Lord of Power to all the children of men in the former Book, as is recorded therein where He saith "I go away and come again."
But when He came, the people of the earth denied Him, save those who were endowed with vision from God, the Lord of all worlds.

order.why: Examine the reported interpretation involving two successive Manifestations.
Conclude the linked sequence with the explicit identification of the Báb and Bahá’u’lláh.
shortened: Concerning what you wrote about the second coming of Christ, that there are differences among the friends - Glory be to God! Time and again it has flowed from the pen of 'Abdu'l-Baha and has been explicitly and conclusively declared that what is meant in the prophecies by the Lord of Hosts and the Promised Christ is the Blessed Beauty and the Exalted One [the Bab], and the beliefs of all must be centered on this explicit and conclusive text.

order.why: Consider the request for evidence concerning the Kingdom.
shortened: O thou seeker after Truth! Thy letter was received and thy purpose became known. Thou hast asked: If this divine Revelation is that same heavenly Kingdom which Christ said was nigh, then by what proof and testimony can this be demonstrated, and by what tidings can it be announced?

order.why: Read the New Jerusalem image with its supplied boundaries visible.
Close with an address to a reader who has acknowledged the claimed return.
shortened: O handmaiden of God who is attracted! Open your tongue in thanksgiving to the Lord God, for praise be to God, you have heard the commandments, counsels and teachings of Baha'u'llah and have acknowledged and recognized the return of Christ.

questions: What assumptions about identity are involved in recognizing a person’s return, and how do these selections change that question?
How does the example of Elijah and John help interpret return, and what further reasoning is needed before applying it to another claim?
What different readings might the ascension passage in Acts sustain when considered alongside the language of heaven in this compilation?
How can one investigate signs and claims of fulfillment without allowing either a fixed expectation or a wish for novelty to settle the matter in advance?
What would recognition mean for conduct and relationships, beyond arriving at an interpretation?

neighbors.invitation: Follow the appeal to read the Gospel as part of assessing the proclamation.
Compare the language of first and last with continuity across revelations.
Consider the responsibilities of discussion when readers reach different conclusions.

references.label: 1 · Acts 1:9–11 (King James Version)
references.note: The account describes Jesus being taken from the disciples’ sight by a cloud and the promise that he will return in a corresponding manner. Read its concrete narrative details alongside the compilation’s interpretations of heaven and clouds. The comparison makes the interpretive problem visible rather than assuming that the narrative itself establishes the Bahá’í reading.

references.label: 2 · Matthew 17:10–13 (King James Version)
references.note: After Jesus speaks of Elijah having already come without being recognized, the disciples understand him to mean John the Baptist. Compare this episode with the use of Elijah and John in the compilation. It provides a specific scriptural example for reflection on return; identifying the implications for a later claimant requires an additional argument.

subjects.displayTitle: The Seal of the Prophets: finality and fulfillment
subjects.introduction: Bahá’u’lláh calls Muhammad the Seal of the Prophets with unreserved reverence, the one for whom God made the world a ring upon His finger, after whom no one may claim the station of prophethood. He also announces that the verse naming Muhammad the Seal has found its consummation in the Day when mankind stands before the Lord of the worlds. To hold those two statements together without hurrying past their tension is the task of this subject. What does completion mean, and what does it leave open? The Qur’án’s own wording, read in parallel translations, is where the disagreement actually lies [1], and the tradition in which Muhammad likens himself to the final brick in a beautiful house gives finality a positive content that deserves to be heard in its own terms [2]. Against that stands the Íqán’s argument that the Prophets share one station, so that He Who is first is also last, and the claim that at the moment of manifestation no allusion profits and the Sovereign is known only through Himself. The inquiry continues into the life of Muhammad, the character of Islam, and the ways prophecy is fulfilled.
subjects.arc: Begin with honor for Muhammad, place explicit statements of finality together, and then work through the compilation’s account of consummation and renewed revelation.

order.why: Explore the Íqán’s interpretation of first and last through unity of station.
shortened: Hath not Muhammad, Himself, declared: "I am all the Prophets"? Hath He not said as We have already mentioned: "I am Adam, Noah, Moses, and Jesus"? Why should Muhammad, that immortal Beauty, Who hath said: "I am the first Adam" be incapable of saying also: "I am the last Adam"? For even as He regarded Himself to be the "First of the Prophets" -- that is Adam -- in like manner, the "Seal of the Prophets" is also applicable unto that Divine Beauty. It is admittedly obvious that being the "First of the Prophets," He likewise is their "Seal."

order.why: Begin with the purpose attributed to Muhammad’s mission: unity and human benefit.
Read the blessing upon Muhammad and the associated call to harmony.
Pause over the honor expressed through the image of the world as a ring.
Establish the affirmation of the prophetic chain reaching its seal.
shortened: And from among humanity He sent forth certain souls who were sanctified from the conditions, veils, allusions and indications of creation, dispatching them with the royal seal of "I am the Truth" and sending them to guide mankind.

And this holy, blessed, and exalted chain ended with the Seal of the Prophets and King of the Chosen Ones, through whom the gate of heaven was opened and the Nightingale of Eternity sang upon the branches of the Divine Lote-Tree that which the Tongue of Grandeur had spoken before the existence of all things: Verily there is no God but Him, the All-Knowing, the All-Wise.

order.why: Read the explicit statement about the sealing of prophethood and messengership.
shortened: See that which the All-Merciful hath revealed therein: 'Verily He is the Messenger of God, and the Seal of the Prophets.'"

To this We reply: "Indeed thou speaketh the truth. We do testify that through Him, Messengership and Prophethood have both been sealed and any one claiming after Him this most exalted station is in manifest error.

order.why: Consider the affirmation of the Qur’ánic designation.
Hear the Báb’s reported public affirmation of Muhammad and the Imams.
shortened: The condemnation of God be also upon whosoever imputes to me the charge of having denied the unity of God, of having repudiated the prophethood of Muhammad, the Seal of the Prophets, of having rejected the truth of any of the messengers of old, or of having refused to recognize the guardianship of Ali, the Commander of the Faithful, or of any of the imams who have succeeded him.

order.why: Examine the juxtaposition of the Seal with the promised day of meeting God.
Follow the distinction between sealed prophethood and the appearance described here.
shortened: They have not yet understood the meaning of "Seal of the Prophets" as revealed in the Qur'an, for it is clear and evident that after the ending of Prophethood, both implicitly and explicitly, the appearance of God is mentioned and recorded in the Divine Book.

One day, amongst the companions, both resident and pilgrim, the Tongue of Grandeur spoke these words: "This is the Day which hath been announced in His saying, exalted be He: 'The Day when thy Lord shall come.' Those who are possessed of insight can perceive that if, in this Day, any soul should cling to or seek after any one of the Names, he would be accounted among the idolaters."

order.why: Discusses the Seal of the Prophets in relation to acknowledgment of prophetic revelation without beginning or end.
Read the consummation language in relation to standing before God.
shortened: Verily We have given glad-tidings unto all people that the great and blessed verse "but He is the Apostle of God and the Seal of the Prophets" hath been fulfilled in the Day when mankind shall stand before the Lord of the worlds.

order.why: Consider a further statement of that relationship.
shortened: In this day the Sun of Truth, from the horizon of the prison of 'Akka, speaketh this most sublime Word: I say in truth, the blessed word "but He is the Apostle of God and the Seal of the Prophets" found its consummation in "the Day when mankind shall stand before the Lord of the worlds."

order.why: Turn to the direct announcement that the prophetic cycle has ended.
shortened: It is evident that every age in which a Manifestation of God hath lived is divinely ordained, and may, in a sense, be characterized as God’s appointed Day. This Day, however, is unique, and is to be distinguished from those that have preceded it. The designation “Seal of the Prophets” fully revealeth its high station. The Prophetic Cycle hath, verily, ended. The Eternal Truth is now come.

order.why: Read the Báb’s account of completion and fulfillment.
shortened: When God sent forth His Prophet Muhammad, on that day the termination of the prophetic cycle was foreordained in the knowledge of God. Yea, that promise hath indeed come true and the decree of God hath been accomplished as He hath ordained.

subjects.displayTitle: Christian teachings and practices: belief brought into life
subjects.introduction: Keep the Beatitudes and the Lord’s Prayer, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says, and the Gospel will have done its work in you; the trouble begins when belief is professed and the life denies it, when nations that pray for their enemies slaughter them by the hundred thousand. The subject is Christianity measured by the conduct it produces. That measure reaches the Supper, a heavenly meal rather than one of bread and wine; the diverging accounts of who Christ was, which turned into strife; the claims of priests, the customs of images and bells, and the gulf between Christ’s admonitions and the administration of the Vatican. The Chalcedonian definition of one Christ in two natures [1] and the Catholic explanation of Eucharistic presence [2] let two traditions state their doctrine in their own exact language, so that a critique can be weighed against what is actually believed. Where this leads is toward the return of Christ and His second coming, toward the standing of the Christian clergy, and toward the meaning of the cross and the Trinity.
subjects.arc: Begin with teachings put into practice, explore spiritual nourishment and doctrine, and then examine the relationships among custom, authority, disagreement, and renewal.

subjects.displayTitle: Persecution of Christians: faith, power, and endurance
subjects.introduction: Fishermen, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá reminds us, were laughed at for believing in Christ: what station could such people have? Yet it was their ensigns that were raised in the end while the standards of the Pharisees toppled, and the apostles who were mocked, beaten unconscious, dragged outside the city and finally crucified became the founders of a civilization. The persecution of the early Christians raises a question that outlives its period: why does a community with no public power become a lasting spiritual force, and why do the learned and the powerful so often fail to see what the humble see? Bahá’u’lláh answers in part by pointing to the expectations of the day, a Messiah with David’s throne and armies rather than a despised man on a donkey, and to teachers who read the Torah according to their own desires. The Pharisees, though, were never a single uniform actor: Gamaliel, one of them, stood before the council and urged it to leave the apostles alone lest it find itself fighting against God [1]. His restraint keeps the accounts of particular opponents from hardening into a verdict on a whole people, and a later story of a Bahá’í family’s suffering shows the pattern recurring across communities. The road leads on to Christ Himself, to the rejection He met, and to the meaning of suffering.
subjects.arc: Begin with the unexpected power of ordinary disciples, consider the costs and causes of opposition, and widen the inquiry toward restraint and comparisons across religious experience.

subjects.introduction: Some call Christ a prophet, some the Word of God, some divine, and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, recalling Bahá’u’lláh’s illustration of conscience, says these schools should not interfere with one another, since each has understood according to its own comprehension. The teaching is not that every account is equally true. It is that understanding is shaped by capacity and conscience, and that quarrelling over the difference adds nothing to anyone’s vision while it destroys the fellowship in which vision grows. Holding a conviction and refusing to fight about it turn out to be compatible, and the second may be the harder discipline. Personal investigation, individual accountability, and differences of capacity place this refusal to quarrel within a larger discipline of inquiry. Paul faced the same problem in Rome over food and holy days, and asked believers to stop despising and judging one another while they still disagreed [1]. From here the road leads toward the independent investigation of truth, which gives each person the dignity of seeing for himself, toward the many meanings a single verse of scripture can hold, and toward the authoritative interpretation that keeps diversity of understanding from becoming division.

references.note: Paul addresses disputes over food and the observance of days, urging believers to welcome one another and refrain from contempt or judgment. The subjects of disagreement differ, so the passage should not be treated as declaring all doctrinal claims equivalent; the comparison concerns the conduct of people who remain in disagreement.
